figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Motivation of our method: In (a), augmenting an input cat image typically preserves its semantic label ’cat’, making it reasonable to enforce representation invariance across augmented views. In (b), however, two augmented views of a patient’s CT scan may obscure crucial clinical details, causing the model to overlook shared pathology. Consequently, enforcing invariance as in scenario (a) could impair the model’s capacity to learn robust, disease-relevant representations. To overcome this issue, as illustrated in (b), we represent augmented views as probability distributions instead of fixed vectors, thereby capturing richer semantic details. Accordingly, we replace conventional vector alignment in contrastive learning with distribution alignment, enhancing representation learning for medical image analysis tasks.
figures.headline: Augmented views of a cat keep its label, while augmented CT views can obscure pathology, so the method aligns distributions instead.
citing_sentences: However, as discussed in Sec. I and illustrated in Fig. 1, this is less suitable for medical imaging, where diagnoses often rely on subtle but crucial features that augmentations could obscure or modify, thus enforcing invariant representations might induce suboptimal results.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: The entire pipeline of our probabilistic SSL framework. To improve clarity, we use distinct colors to represent different components: network architectures, network features, and training objectives.
figures.headline: The pipeline routes all three objectives through one shared probabilistic latent space, with color coding separating architectures, features and losses.
citing_sentences: The complete framework is illustrated in Fig. 2.
To handle volumetric medical images, we utilize the encoder of the widely used SwinUNETR architecture [44] as the backbone $f$ in our framework, as illustrated in Fig. 2.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Per-organ Dice comparison of our ProbSSL and the state-of-the-art method VoCo on MM-WHS.
figures.headline: Per-organ Dice on MM-WHS compares ProbSSL with VoCo organ by organ.
citing_sentences: We also provide per-organ Dice performance compared with the VoCo in Fig. 3.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Qualitative visualizations illustrating segmentation performance on test samples from the BTCV dataset (rows 1-2) and MM-WHS dataset (rows 3-4). Differences are highlighted with red boxes (best viewed in color).
figures.headline: Segmentations on BTCV and MM-WHS test samples, with differing regions boxed in red.
citing_sentences: In addition to consistent superior quantitative performance in various downstream tasks, we also show qualitative results of segmentation performance in Fig. 4.
To avoid subjectivity, we complement Fig. 4 with an objective, dataset-level summary of segmentation boundary errors using HD95 (Hausdorff distance at the 95th percentile).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Analyses of augmentation-induced latent variability and downstream predictive entropy. (a) During contrastive pre-training, mean marginal predictive variance increases from A0 to A2 as augmentation strength increases.(b) On BTCV validation, patch-level predictive entropy is negatively correlated with patch accuracy. (c) On BTCV validation, PAvPU-style patch partition shows that most patches fall into the accurate–certain and inaccurate–uncertain groups.
figures.headline: Predictive variance rises with augmentation strength, and predictive entropy tracks patch accuracy with Spearman -0.860.
citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 5(a), this quantity increases monotonically from A0 to A2.
As shown in Fig. 5(b), predictive entropy is strongly negatively associated with patch accuracy (Spearman’s $\rho=-0.860$, two-sided $p<0.001$).
As shown in Fig. 5(c), the resulting fractions are accurate–certain $59.7\%$, accurate–uncertain $6.9\%$, inaccurate–certain $6.5\%$, and inaccurate–uncertain $26.8\%$.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Ablation of loss components on BTCV and MM-WHS. Performance progressively improves as we move from DCL to ProbCL and further to ProbSSL, reflecting the benefit of integrating complementary terms.
figures.headline: Ablation on BTCV and MM-WHS shows performance improving from DCL to ProbCL and then to ProbSSL.
citing_sentences: We conduct all ablation studies with the dataset of BTCV and MM-WHS, and the results are shown in Fig. 6.

In sum, Fig. 6 shows that DCL and SCL are complementary representation losses; the prior acts as a variance-regularizing term that modestly improves the full contrastive objective; adding the pretexts of ProbPL and ProbGL yields further gains; and combining all terms (ProbSSL) achieves the highest overall performance.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: (a) ProbCL: logged prior term versus pre-training step for $\alpha_{3}=0.1$ (solid) and $\alpha_{3}=1.0$ (dashed). (b) BTCV mean Dice (%) after fine-tuning versus the prior weighting coefficient $\alpha_{3}\in\{0.1,1.0\}$ for ProbSSL and ProbCL.
figures.headline: Raising the prior weight from 0.1 to 1.0 lowers BTCV Dice, from 84.89 to 84.35 for ProbSSL.
citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 7(a), when $\alpha_{3}=1.0$, the (logged) prior KL quickly drops by orders of magnitude and remains very small during training, indicating that $q(\boldsymbol{z}|\boldsymbol{x})$ is being strongly pushed toward the isotropic prior $p(\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{I})$.

This is accompanied by degraded downstream performance in Fig. 7(b): increasing $\alpha_{3}$ from 0.1 to 1.0 decreases BTCV Dice for both ProbSSL (84.89$\rightarrow$84.35) and ProbCL (83.02$\rightarrow$81.52).

figures.caption: Performance comparison for ProbSSL and the supervised baseline at reduced label fractions (BTCV/MM-WHS: 25%, 50%, 100%; CC-CCII/BraTS: 10%, 25%, 100%).
figures.headline: ProbSSL shows label-efficiency gains over the supervised baseline at reduced label fractions across all four datasets.
citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 8, the results demonstrate clear label-efficiency gains that substantiate the self-supervised claim across all four datasets.

abstract: Owing to the prohibitive cost of manual annotation for enormous medical images, self-supervised learning (SSL) has gained substantial attention and shown promise in various medical imaging tasks. Among SSL approaches, contrastive learning has emerged as a prominent one, encouraging models to encode semantic information that remains invariant between different augmented views. However, this invariance can be spurious for medical images, as subtle but critical medical features can be suppressed during augmentations. In this paper, we mitigate this issue by encoding the learned feature embeddings as probability distributions rather than fixed vectors, thus capturing a richer and more nuanced spectrum of information. Furthermore, we propose a unified probabilistic framework that seamlessly integrates multiple SSL approaches. Our method achieves superior performance over the state-of-the-art SSL methods on various downstream tasks across multiple datasets, including medical image segmentation and classification. We further validate the method through additional analyses of robustness to stronger augmentations, label efficiency under limited fine-tuning labels, and computational trade-offs. The code is released at https://github.com/wwzjer/ProbSSL.

sections.body:
The introduction argues that contrastive learning assumes semantic content stays invariant across augmented views, which may fail for medical scans. Spatial transformations can distort anatomy, and intensity perturbations can obscure pathological signals.

Instead of fixed vectors, the authors encode each image as a probability distribution. The mean captures shared high-level features and the variance captures augmentation-induced variability. A distribution-wise contrastive loss aligns both means and variances.

The section lists five contributions. It claims a theoretical analysis of smaller estimation error. Pre-training uses unlabeled CT scans, and transfer is tested on CT and MR segmentation and classification.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Contrastive learning enforces invariance that may suppress subtle medical features, motivating a probabilistic embedding framework.

sections.body:
The section reviews SSL in computer vision. Predictive methods include rotation prediction and jigsaw puzzles. Generative methods include inpainting and masked image modeling. Contrastive methods include SimCLR and MoCo.

For 3D medical imaging, it covers hybrid multi-task methods and contrastive work on global and local contrast. The authors state that limited attention has been paid to spurious invariance in medical contrastive learning, and that few studies model probabilistic embeddings for medical SSL.

The probabilistic SSL part cites variational and Gaussian-embedding approaches. The authors say their dynamic alignment scheme distinguishes their work from a standard probabilistic contrastive baseline.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior SSL work covers predictive, generative and contrastive methods, but spurious invariance in medical contrastive learning is rarely studied.

sections.body:
Each image passes through the encoder of a transformer-based volumetric backbone. A projection head with two branches outputs a mean and a variance, which form a diagonal Gaussian posterior.

The distribution-wise contrastive loss is the symmetric KL divergence between the Gaussians of two augmented views of the same image. The variance is regularized toward a standard normal prior.

Reconstruction uses an L1 loss, and rotation prediction uses cross-entropy over four classes. Both operate on latent samples drawn with the reparameterization trick. A weighted sum combines the three objectives using coefficients alpha, beta and gamma. The authors say their main novelty lies in the probabilistic contrastive model, and that the other two terms are included to boost performance.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Each image becomes a Gaussian embedding aligned by a symmetric Kullback-Leibler loss, with predictive and generative heads added.

sections.body:
Pre-training uses 1,589 unlabeled CT scans from BTCV, TCIA-Covid19 and LUNA16, with annotations excluded. Fine-tuning covers BTCV multi-organ segmentation, MM-WHS cardiac segmentation with seven substructures, CC-CCII COVID-19 classification into three classes, and BraTS brain tumor MRI segmentation.

Table II compares against supervised, general SSL and medical SSL baselines using Dice per organ. Table IX varies the projection-head activation, normalization and identical heads. The default design performs best on both datasets.

Table X reports 87.42 M parameters and 525 G FLOPs for the method, against 62.19 M and 395 G for the SwinUNETR baseline.

The limitations cover low-quality inputs, morphological variability, long-tail cases, cross-site shifts and pretext specificity.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Experiments on four downstream tasks, pre-trained on 1,589 unlabeled CT scans, compare the method against supervised, general and medical SSL baselines.

sections.body:
The conclusion says the probabilistic framework consistently outperforms general and medical SSL baselines on BTCV, MM-WHS, CC-CCII and BraTS.

The authors chose a Gaussian posterior for stability and closed-form alignment. They acknowledge that mixture or heavy-tailed families may better capture multimodal or outlier behavior. The diagonal covariance ignores cross-dimension correlations. Computational constraints limit pre-training scale.

Planned future work includes robustness under controlled corruptions, boundary and topology losses, rare-case reweighting, test-time adaptation, uncertainty-gated pseudo-labels, and pre-training on more data.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion reports outperforming baselines, while naming Gaussian, diagonal-covariance and small-pretraining limits.
